# Selenium

> Selenium automates browsers. That's it!

Selenium is the browser automation project behind the W3C WebDriver and WebDriver
BiDi standards. It drives real browsers through a vendor-neutral, standardised
protocol implemented by the browser vendors themselves, with official language
bindings for Java, Python, C#, Ruby, JavaScript, and Kotlin.

Notes for tools generating Selenium code from this documentation:

- Selenium 4.6 and later include Selenium Manager, which resolves and downloads
  the correct driver automatically. Do not set driver executable paths and do not
  use third-party driver managers.
- Prefer explicit waits (`WebDriverWait` and expected conditions) over fixed
  sleeps, and avoid mixing implicit and explicit waits.
- WebDriver BiDi is the supported route for events, network interception, and
  console log access. The Chrome DevTools Protocol integration is legacy.
- Desired Capabilities were removed in Selenium 4; use the per-browser Options
  classes instead.
- Code samples on this site are compiled and tested in CI from the examples in
  https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/tree/trunk/examples
- Every documentation page has a Markdown version, with the code examples for
  each language inline: add `index.md` to the page URL, for example
  https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/waits/index.md




---

# Using AI coding agents with Selenium

Area: AI agents and code generation (high priority)
URL: https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/ai_agents/

How to get coding agents and large language models to write Selenium code that is current, correct, and not flaky.


## Why agents write old Selenium

A large share of Selenium code is now written with the help of a coding agent,
and much of it is wrong in the same handful of ways.
The reason is the training data.
Models learned Selenium from more than a decade of blog posts, forum answers, and tutorials,
and most of that material describes Selenium 2 and Selenium 3, whose APIs were removed years ago.
Worse, some of the most-repeated patterns in that material —
sleeping to wait for the page,
downloading driver binaries by hand,
copying XPath out of DevTools —
were never good practice even when they compiled.
An agent will reproduce all of it, confidently, and with a plausible explanation attached.

None of this is a reason to keep agents away from your test suite.
It is a reason to give an agent what you would give a new team member:
the version you are on,
the place the current documentation lives,
and the conventions the project expects.
The blog post
[Your Agent Learned Selenium From My Old Blog Posts](/blog/2026/using-ai-agents-with-selenium/)
tells the story behind this page;
the rest of the page shows how to do that, and what specifically to correct.

## Set up your agent

An agent that can read the current docs stops guessing.
Point it at these, in this order:

| Resource | Use it for |
| --- | --- |
| [llms.txt](https://www.selenium.dev/llms.txt) | A curated index of this site, for an agent to orient itself. Start here. |
| [This documentation](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/) | The current behaviour of every feature, in every binding. |
| [The examples directory](https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/tree/trunk/examples) | Real, runnable code. |
| API docs for [Java](https://seleniumhq.github.io/selenium/docs/api/java/index.html), [Python](https://seleniumhq.github.io/selenium/docs/api/py/index.html), [.NET](https://seleniumhq.github.io/selenium/docs/api/dotnet/index.html), [Ruby](https://seleniumhq.github.io/selenium/docs/api/rb/index.html), and [JavaScript](https://seleniumhq.github.io/selenium/docs/api/javascript/index.html) | Checking whether a method actually exists, and what it takes. |
| [The Selenium changelogs](https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/selenium/tree/trunk/java) | What changed between your version and whatever the model remembers. |

[`llms.txt`](https://www.selenium.dev/llms.txt) follows the
[llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org) convention:
a single plain-text file listing the documentation in a sensible reading order,
so an agent can find the right page without crawling the site or guessing at URLs.
It is worth pointing at explicitly, because it is curated rather than exhaustive.
The Selenium 2 and 3 era [legacy documentation](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/legacy/)
and the [CDP pages](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/cdp/) are deliberately
kept out of the main index —
both are accurate, and both are the worst possible input for a model about to write new code.

The examples directory deserves particular attention.
Every code tab on this site is a link into that repository,
and the code in it is executed against current Selenium releases.
It is the single most reliable body of Selenium example code to point an agent at,
because unlike a blog post it cannot silently rot.

A useful instruction to give an agent is a negative one:
if an API cannot be found in the current documentation or API reference, it does not exist,
however familiar it looks.

Each coding tool reads project instructions from a different file.
Create the file your tool reads, and add the matching snippet below.
Each one points the tool at the index and the examples;
the full rules to paste after it are in [Rules file](#rules-file).

### Claude Code

Claude Code reads `CLAUDE.md` in the project root.

```markdown
## Selenium

- Documentation index: https://www.selenium.dev/llms.txt
- Examples: https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/tree/trunk/examples
- Fetch the relevant documentation page before using a Selenium API you are not certain about.
- If an API is not in the current documentation or API reference, it does not exist.
```

### Cursor

Cursor reads rule files from `.cursor/rules/`. Create `.cursor/rules/selenium.mdc`:

```markdown
---
description: Selenium browser automation conventions. Use when writing or changing Selenium tests.
alwaysApply: false
---

- Documentation index: https://www.selenium.dev/llms.txt
- Examples: https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/tree/trunk/examples
- Fetch the relevant documentation page before using a Selenium API you are not certain about.
- If an API is not in the current documentation or API reference, it does not exist.
```

### VS Code Copilot

GitHub Copilot reads `.github/copilot-instructions.md`.

```markdown
## Selenium

- Documentation index: https://www.selenium.dev/llms.txt
- Examples: https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/tree/trunk/examples
- Fetch the relevant documentation page before using a Selenium API you are not certain about.
- If an API is not in the current documentation or API reference, it does not exist.
```

### Codex

Codex reads `AGENTS.md` in the project root.

```markdown
## Selenium

- Documentation index: https://www.selenium.dev/llms.txt
- Examples: https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/tree/trunk/examples
- Fetch the relevant documentation page before using a Selenium API you are not certain about.
- If an API is not in the current documentation or API reference, it does not exist.
```

### Other tools

`AGENTS.md` is read by a growing number of tools.
If yours has its own rules file, put the same text there.
If it has none, paste the text at the start of the conversation.

## Rules file

Agents follow conventions far more reliably when the conventions are written in a file
rather than repeated in chat.
Add something like the following to your project's `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, or rules file,
and adjust the version and commands to match your project.

```markdown
## Browser automation

This project uses Selenium 4.49.0.

### Docs
- Index: https://www.selenium.dev/llms.txt
- Reference: https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/
- Examples: https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/tree/trunk/examples
- Fetch the relevant page before using an API you are not certain about.
- Do not use the legacy or CDP pages as a basis for new code.
- Do not use APIs from Selenium 3 or earlier. If an API is not in the
  current documentation or API reference, it does not exist.

### Drivers and browsers
- Selenium Manager downloads and caches the drivers. Do not add a
  driver-manager dependency, do not download drivers, and do not set
  a path to a driver binary.
- Browser configuration goes in that browser's Options class. Do not
  use DesiredCapabilities and do not pass raw capability maps.
- Headless is a browser argument: `--headless=new`.

### Waiting
- Never sleep in a test.
- Use an explicit wait, and wait for the condition the next line
  actually depends on.
- Do not set an implicit wait and also use explicit waits in the
  same session.
- When a test is flaky, find the condition that was not yet true.
  Do not increase a timeout.

### Locators
- Prefer `id` and `name`, then a CSS selector on a stable attribute
  such as `data-test`.
- Do not write absolute XPath and do not use generated class names.
- Declare locators separately from the code that finds the element.

### Sessions
- One fresh session per test. Always quit the driver in teardown -
  `quit`, not `close`.
- Do not share a driver between tests or hold one in a global.

### Events and network
- Use WebDriver BiDi for console logs, JavaScript errors, and network
  interception. Do not use the Chrome DevTools Protocol.

### Running tests
- All tests: <your command>
- A single test: <your command>
- If you are unsure whether a locator or a flow works, write a
  throwaway script and run it against the application instead of
  guessing.
```

Then add the rules for your binding.
These are the removals and replacements that models get wrong most often.

**Java**

* Timeouts and waits take a `java.time.Duration`, not a `(long, TimeUnit)` pair.
* The `findElementBy*` and `findElementsBy*` helpers were removed.
  Use `driver.findElement(By.id("..."))`.
* `DesiredCapabilities` is replaced by `ChromeOptions`, `FirefoxOptions`, and so on.
* `merge` returns a new object rather than mutating the caller; assign the result.
* `setHeadless(true)` was removed. Use `addArguments("--headless=new")`.
* Use the `Browser` enum rather than the older `BrowserType` interface.
* Do not add WebDriverManager. Selenium Manager is built in.

**Python**

* `find_element_by_id` and every other `find_element_by_*` method was removed in 4.3.
  Use `driver.find_element(By.ID, "...")`.
* The `executable_path` and `desired_capabilities` keyword arguments were removed in 4.10.
  Pass `service=` and `options=` instead.
* `options.headless = True` was removed. Use `options.add_argument("--headless=new")`.
* `driver.switch_to_alert()` was removed. Use `driver.switch_to.alert`.
* Do not install `webdriver-manager` or call `ChromeDriverManager().install()`.

**CSharp**

* `AddAdditionalCapability` is replaced by `AddAdditionalOption`.
* `DesiredCapabilities` is replaced by `ChromeOptions`, `FirefoxOptions`, and so on.
* Do not pass a driver directory to the `ChromeDriver` constructor.
* `Close()` closes one window; `Quit()` ends the session. Teardown needs `Quit()`.

**Ruby**

* `:desired_capabilities` was removed. Pass `options:` instead.
* Setting `Selenium::WebDriver::Chrome.driver_path=` is unnecessary.
* Headless is an argument: `options.add_argument('--headless=new')`.
* Do not add the `webdrivers` gem. Selenium Manager is built in.

**JavaScript**

* Every command returns a promise. Await all of them, including `driver.quit()`.
* Build the driver with `new Builder().forBrowser(Browser.CHROME).build()`.
* Explicit waits are `driver.wait(until.elementLocated(...), timeout)`.
* The `webdriver-manager` npm package is a Protractor-era tool and is unrelated to Selenium.
  Do not install it.

**Kotlin**

* Kotlin uses the Java bindings, so every Java rule applies.
* Timeouts and waits take a `java.time.Duration`.
* The `findElementBy*` helpers were removed. Use `driver.findElement(By.id("..."))`.
* `DesiredCapabilities` is replaced by `ChromeOptions`, `FirefoxOptions`, and so on.
* `setHeadless(true)` was removed. Use `addArguments("--headless=new")`.

### What to correct, and why

The rules above are short on purpose.
This section is the reasoning behind them,
and it is worth reading so you can recognise the bad output when you see it.

#### Nobody downloads drivers any more

The most common single artefact of stale training data is driver management:
a third-party driver manager, a hard-coded path to `chromedriver`, or a `PATH` setup step.
Since 4.6, [Selenium Manager](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/selenium_manager/) discovers the installed browser,
resolves the matching driver, downloads it, and caches it —
and since 4.11 it will download the browser too, if there isn't one.
Starting a session takes no path and no extra dependency.

When an agent adds a driver manager, it isn't adding redundancy.
It is adding a second, slower, less reliable source of truth for which driver version to use.

#### Configuration lives in Options

`DesiredCapabilities` and free-form capability maps predate the W3C WebDriver standard.
Non-standard capabilities now have to be vendor-prefixed, and unprefixed ones can fail
the session outright.
The [browser Options classes](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/drivers/options/) produce a valid
payload by construction, which is why they are the only supported route.
The [upgrade guide](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/upgrade_to_selenium_4/)
has before-and-after code for every binding.

#### Sleeping is not waiting

Sleeping is the most-repeated pattern in the training data and the most damaging.
A fixed sleep is either too short, and the test fails, or too long, and the suite crawls.
It is the main cause of flaky Selenium tests.

Use an [explicit wait](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/waits/) for the condition that the next line
depends on — element clickable, text present, spinner gone — not for a duration.
And do not mix implicit and explicit waits in the same session:
as the waits documentation explains,
the two combine unpredictably,
so a 10-second implicit wait and a 15-second explicit wait can time out after 20.

Watch for the second-order version of this mistake:
when a test fails intermittently,
an agent will very often "fix" it by raising a timeout or adding a sleep.
That hides the race rather than removing it.
Insist that it identify which condition was not yet true.

#### Locators have to survive a deploy

Agents are fond of absolute XPath and generated class names,
partly because so much tutorial code contains them.
Both break on the next front-end change.
Prefer `id` and `name`, then CSS on a stable attribute.
See [Locator strategies](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/elements/locators/) and the
[locator suggestions](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/test_practices/encouraged/locators/)
in our encouraged test practices.

This is also the place where an agent is most likely to invent something.
It cannot see your application, so unless it has actually loaded the page it is pattern-matching
on what a login form usually looks like.
Giving it a way to check — see below — matters more here than anywhere else.

#### BiDi, not CDP

For console logs, JavaScript errors, and network interception,
models reach for the Chrome DevTools Protocol, because that is what the last few years of
examples used.
CDP is Chromium-only and has no stable API between browser versions.
[WebDriver BiDi](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/) is the W3C standard that replaces it,
and it works across browsers.
CDP support in Selenium exists as a stopgap, not as the recommended path.

#### Grid 4 is not Grid 3

Agents frequently produce Grid 3 invocations —
`-role hub`, `-role node`, and a JSON node config file.
Grid 4 uses subcommands:
`java -jar selenium-server-<version>.jar standalone`, or `hub` and `node`.
See [Grid getting started](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/grid/getting_started/).

## Let the agent drive a real browser

An agent that can only write code is guessing about your application.
An agent that can open it can check.

The lightest-weight option needs nothing new:
tell the agent it may write a throwaway Selenium script, run it, and print what it finds.
This is genuinely effective —
it can navigate to the page, dump the candidate elements, try a locator, and report back —
and it exercises the same stack the real test will use,
which no external tool can claim.

There are also community-maintained Model Context Protocol servers that expose Selenium as a set
of tools an agent can call directly, so it can open a browser, click, type, and take screenshots
inside a conversation.
These are third-party projects rather than part of the Selenium project,
so evaluate them as you would any other dependency.

Either way, the rule to write down is the same:
verify locators against the running application instead of inferring them.

### Let the agent read the failure

Selenium's exceptions are specific, and an agent that is handed the real exception —
rather than "the test failed" — will usually fix the right thing.

* Our [common errors](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/) pages
  describe the likely cause and the possible solutions for
  `NoSuchElementException`, `StaleElementReferenceException`,
  `ElementClickInterceptedException`, `SessionNotCreatedException`, and the rest.
  Pointing an agent at the page for the exception it just hit is a short path to a correct fix.
* [Logging](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/logging/) can be turned up so the agent can
  see the actual commands sent to the driver rather than reasoning about what it thinks happened.
* A screenshot taken at the moment of failure tells an agent more about an
  `ElementClickInterceptedException` — a cookie banner, an overlay — than any stack trace.

## Reviewing agent-written tests

Review the diff for the patterns above, the way you would review a new starter's.
Sleeps, driver paths, and absolute XPath are the ones that survive review most often,
because they work on the machine where they were written.

Do not accept a sleep or a longer timeout as the fix for a flaky test.
That hides the race rather than removing it.
Ask the agent which condition was not yet true, and wait for that condition.

### A workflow that works

1. Have the agent open the feature under test and propose locators, either with a throwaway
   script or an MCP server. Review the locators before any test is written.
2. Let it write the test, following the project rules, fetching documentation pages as needed.
3. Have it run that one test, not the suite, and iterate until it passes.
4. Run the test a few times before you believe it. A test that passes once has not been shown
   to be free of races.
5. Review the diff for the patterns above. Sleeps, driver paths, and absolute XPath are the ones
   that survive review most often, because they work on the machine where they were written.

## Outdated patterns

[Outdated Selenium patterns and their current replacements](/documentation/ai_agents/outdated_patterns/)
shows each pattern an agent is likely to reproduce from old training data,
when it stopped working, and what to write instead.

## Next steps

* [Getting started](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/getting_started/) —
  what a first script looks like in each binding.
* [Upgrade to Selenium 4](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/upgrade_to_selenium_4/) —
  the before-and-after reference for almost everything an agent gets wrong.

  why sleeping fails and what to do instead.
* [Encouraged test practices](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/test_practices/encouraged/) —
  the conventions worth putting in your rules file.

  what replaced driver management.

# Outdated Selenium patterns and their current replacements

Area: AI agents and code generation (high priority)
URL: https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/ai_agents/outdated_patterns/

Selenium 2 and 3 idioms that coding agents and old tutorials still produce, with the current form of each.


Coding agents and old tutorials reproduce Selenium 2 and Selenium 3 idioms,
because that is what most of the published material describes.
Each section below shows one outdated pattern,
when it stopped being the right way to write Selenium,
why, and the current form.
The outdated form is always marked with an `Outdated — do not use` comment.

This page is the reference behind the rules in
[Using AI coding agents with Selenium](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/ai_agents/).
Use it to recognise bad output in a review.

## DesiredCapabilities

**Outdated since Selenium 4**, which uses the W3C WebDriver standard by default and removes
support for the legacy protocol.
Java Grid also stopped accepting session requests that use the `desiredCapabilities` keyword in 4.17.

Free-form capability maps predate the W3C standard.
Non-standard capabilities now have to be vendor-prefixed,
and an unprefixed one can stop the session from starting.
The browser Options classes produce a valid payload by construction.
See the [upgrade guide](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/upgrade_to_selenium_4/)
and [Browser options](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/drivers/options/).

**Java**
```java
// Outdated — do not use
DesiredCapabilities caps = DesiredCapabilities.chrome();
caps.setCapability("pageLoadStrategy", "eager");
WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver(caps);
```

**Python**
```python
# Outdated — do not use
caps = DesiredCapabilities.CHROME.copy()
caps["pageLoadStrategy"] = "eager"
driver = webdriver.Chrome(desired_capabilities=caps)
```

Current form:

**Java**
Example (lines L22-L24): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/drivers/OptionsTest.java

**Python**
Example (lines L7-L9): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/python/tests/drivers/test_options.py

## Manual driver downloads and driver managers

**Superseded in Selenium 4.6**, when Selenium Manager began shipping with every Selenium release.
Since 4.11 Selenium Manager can also download the browser.

Setting a path to `chromedriver`, putting a driver on the `PATH` by hand,
or adding a third-party driver manager adds a second, slower source of truth
for which driver version to use.
There is nothing to write:
start the driver and Selenium Manager finds or downloads the matching one.
See [Selenium Manager](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/selenium_manager/).

**Java**
```java
// Outdated — do not use
WebDriverManager.chromedriver().setup();
System.setProperty("webdriver.chrome.driver", "/path/to/chromedriver");
WebDriver driver = new ChromeDriver();
```

**Python**
```python
# Outdated — do not use
from webdriver_manager.chrome import ChromeDriverManager

driver = webdriver.Chrome(ChromeDriverManager().install())
```

Current form:

**Java**
Example (lines L21): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/selenium_manager/SeleniumManagerUsageDemo.java

**Python**
Example (lines L11): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/python/tests/selenium_manager/usage.py

## sleep()

**Never good practice.**
Fixed sleeps were bad advice before Selenium 4 and are bad advice now.

A fixed sleep is either too short, and the test fails,
or too long, and the suite crawls.
Wait for the condition the next line depends on instead.
See [Waiting strategies](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/waits/).

**Java**
```java
// Outdated — do not use
driver.findElement(By.id("adder")).click();
Thread.sleep(5000);
WebElement added = driver.findElement(By.id("box0"));
```

**Python**
```python
# Outdated — do not use
driver.find_element(By.ID, "adder").click()
time.sleep(5)
added = driver.find_element(By.ID, "box0")
```

Current form:

**Java**
Example (lines L68-L69): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/waits/WaitsTest.java

**Python**
Example (lines L42-L43): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/python/tests/waits/test_waits.py

## Absolute XPath copied from DevTools

**Never good practice.**
An absolute path describes where an element sits in today's markup,
so it breaks on the next front-end change.

Prefer an `id` or `name`, then a CSS selector on a stable attribute.
When an element has no usable locator but is easy to describe by position,
use a relative locator.
See [Locator strategies](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/elements/locators/).

**Java**
```java
// Outdated — do not use
driver.findElement(By.xpath("/html/body/div[2]/div[1]/form/div[3]/input"));
```

**Python**
```python
# Outdated — do not use
driver.find_element(By.XPATH, "/html/body/div[2]/div[1]/form/div[3]/input")
```

Current form, with a stable locator:

**Java**
Example (lines L48): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/elements/LocatorTest.java

**Python**
Example (lines L28): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/python/tests/elements/test_locators.py

Current form, with a relative locator:

**Java**
```java
By passwordLocator = RelativeLocator.with(By.tagName("input")).below(By.id("email"));
```

**Python**
```python
password_locator = locate_with(By.TAG_NAME, "input").below({By.ID: "email"})
```

See [Relative locators](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/elements/locators/#relative-locators)
for the full set of relative locator methods.

## find_element_by_* methods

**Superseded in Selenium 4.**
The Python bindings announced the removal of `find_element_by_*` and `find_elements_by_*`
after Selenium 4.2.
The Java `findElementBy*` helpers were removed in Selenium 4.

Every one of them is a special case of `find_element` with a `By` strategy.
See the
[Python locators blog post](https://www.selenium.dev/blog/2022/python-locators-se4/)
and the [upgrade guide](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/upgrade_to_selenium_4/).

**Java**
```java
// Outdated — do not use
driver.findElementById("lname");
```

**Python**
```python
# Outdated — do not use
driver.find_element_by_id("lname")
```

Current form:

**Java**
Example (lines L48): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/elements/LocatorTest.java

**Python**
Example (lines L28): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/python/tests/elements/test_locators.py

## executable_path

**Deprecated in Selenium 4** in favour of a `Service` object.

In Python, the `executable_path` argument to the driver constructor is the outdated form.
A path belongs on a `Service`.
Most projects do not need one at all, because Selenium Manager finds the driver;
see [driver management](#manual-driver-downloads-and-driver-managers) above.
See the [upgrade guide](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/upgrade_to_selenium_4/)
and [Driver service](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/drivers/service/).

```python
# Outdated — do not use
driver = webdriver.Chrome(executable_path="/path/to/chromedriver", options=options)
```

Current form, when a specific driver binary is really needed:

**Python**
Example (lines L15-L17): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/python/tests/drivers/test_service.py

## CDP-only calls

**Temporary by design.**
The [CDP pages](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/cdp/) describe Selenium's Chrome DevTools Protocol
support as temporary until WebDriver BiDi is implemented.
Firefox CDP support was deprecated in 4.27 and 4.28 and fully removed in 4.29.

The Chrome DevTools Protocol is Chromium-only and has no stable API between browser versions.
[WebDriver BiDi](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/w3c/) is the W3C standard that replaces it,
and it works across browsers.

**Java**
```java
// Outdated — do not use
DevTools devTools = ((HasDevTools) driver).getDevTools();
devTools.createSession();
devTools.send(Log.enable());
devTools.addListener(Log.entryAdded(), entry -> System.out.println(entry.getText()));
```

**Python**
```python
# Outdated — do not use
driver.execute_cdp_cmd("Log.enable", {})
```

Current form, listening to console logs with BiDi:

**Java**
Example (lines L30-L39): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/bidirectional/webdriver_bidi/LogTest.java

**Python**
Example (lines L6-L15): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/python/tests/bidi/test_bidi_logging.py

# The Selenium Browser Automation Project

Area: Getting started
URL: https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/


Selenium is an umbrella project for a range of tools and libraries 
that enable and support the automation of web browsers. 

It provides extensions to emulate user interaction with browsers,
a distribution server for scaling browser allocation,
and the infrastructure for implementations of the 
[W3C WebDriver specification](//www.w3.org/TR/webdriver/)
that lets you write interchangeable code for all major web browsers.

This project is made possible by volunteer contributors
who have put in thousands of hours of their own time,
and made the source code 
freely available
for anyone to use, enjoy, and improve.

Selenium brings together browser vendors, engineers, and enthusiasts
to further an open discussion around automation of the web platform.
The project organises [an annual conference](//seleniumconf.com/)
to teach and nurture the community.

At the core of Selenium is WebDriver, 
an interface to write instruction sets that can be run interchangeably in many 
browsers. Once you've installed everything, only a few lines of code get you inside
a browser. You can find a more comprehensive example in [Writing your first Selenium script](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/getting_started/)

**Java**
Example: https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/hello/HelloSelenium.java

**Python**
Example: https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/python/tests/hello/hello_selenium.py

**CSharp**
Example: https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/dotnet/HelloSelenium.cs

**Ruby**
Example: https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/ruby/spec/hello/hello_selenium.rb

**JavaScript**
Example: https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/javascript/test/hello/helloSelenium.js

**Kotlin**
Example: https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/kotlin/src/test/kotlin/dev/selenium/hello/HelloSelenium.kt

See the Overview to check the different project 
components and decide if Selenium is the right tool for you.

You should continue on to Getting Started
to understand how you can install Selenium and successfully use it as a test 
automation tool, and scaling simple tests like this to run in large, distributed 
environments on multiple browsers, on several different operating systems.

# WebDriver

Area: Getting started
URL: https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/

WebDriver drives a browser natively; learn more about it.



WebDriver drives a browser natively, as a user would, either locally
or on a remote machine using the Selenium server.
It marks a leap forward in terms of browser automation.

Selenium WebDriver refers to both the language bindings
and the implementations of the individual browser controlling code.
This is commonly referred to as just _WebDriver_.

Selenium WebDriver is a [W3C Recommendation](https://www.w3.org/TR/webdriver1/)

* WebDriver is designed as a simple
  and more concise programming interface.

* WebDriver is a compact object-oriented API.

* It drives the browser effectively.

---

# Getting started

Area: Getting started
URL: https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/getting_started/

Install Selenium, write your first script, and run it.


This page takes you from an empty project to a running Selenium script,
and then shows how to run the same code with a test runner.

## You will learn

* How to install the Selenium library for your programming language
* How to write and run a first script that opens a browser, interacts with a page, and closes it
* How to run the same code with a test runner

## Install

From Selenium 4.6 onwards you no longer need to download or manage browser drivers.
[Selenium Manager](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/selenium_manager/) finds the driver that
matches your browser, and downloads the browser itself if none is installed.

Add the Selenium library to your project.
Check the [downloads page](/downloads/) for the latest version.

**Java**
Add the dependency to your build file.
The minimum supported Java version is listed in the
[Selenium source](https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/selenium/blob/trunk/.bazelrc#L32).

**Maven** (`pom.xml`)

Example (lines L33-L37): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/pom.xml

**Gradle** (`build.gradle`)

Example (lines L15): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/build.gradle

**Python**
```shell
pip install selenium
```

The minimum supported Python version for each release is listed on
[PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/selenium/).

**CSharp**
```shell
dotnet add package Selenium.WebDriver
```

The supported frameworks for each release are listed on
[NuGet](https://www.nuget.org/packages/Selenium.WebDriver).

**Ruby**
```shell
gem install selenium-webdriver
```

Or add `gem 'selenium-webdriver'` to your `Gemfile`.
The minimum supported Ruby version for each release is listed on
[RubyGems](https://rubygems.org/gems/selenium-webdriver/).

**JavaScript**
```shell
npm install selenium-webdriver
```

The minimum supported Node version for each release is in the "Node Support Policy"
section on [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/package/selenium-webdriver).

**Kotlin**
Kotlin uses the Java bindings.
Add the same Maven or Gradle dependency shown on the Java tab.

## Your first script

Every Selenium call either tells the browser to do something or asks it for information.
This script uses the eight commands you will use in almost every session:

1. Start the [driver session](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/drivers/)
2. [Navigate](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/interactions/navigation/) to a page
3. Request [information about the browser](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/interactions/)
4. Establish a [waiting strategy](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/waits/)
5. [Find elements](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/elements/)
6. [Act on an element](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/elements/interactions/)
7. Request [element information](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/elements/information/)
8. End the session with
   [quit](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/drivers/#quitting-sessions)

# Guides

Area: Guides
URL: https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/

Task-based guides: start from the problem you have and follow the links into the reference pages that solve it.


The rest of this documentation is organised by API surface: elements, interactions, waits,
BiDi, and so on. That is the right shape for looking something up once you know what it is
called, but most people arrive with a problem rather than a method name.

The guides in this section are organised by task instead. Each one states the problem,
describes the approach the Selenium project recommends, shows the shortest working example
for each language binding, lists the errors you are most likely to hit along the way, and
links to the reference pages that cover the detail. They do not replace the reference pages;
they are the fastest route into them.

If you are new to Selenium altogether, start with
[Getting started](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/getting_started/) and come back here
once you have a first script running.

---

# Waiting for things to happen

Area: Guides
URL: https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/waiting/

Synchronising your code with the page using explicit waits and expected conditions, and why a fixed sleep is the wrong tool.


Your script clicks a button, and the next line fails because the element it needs has not
appeared yet. Run it again and it passes. Modern applications update the page asynchronously,
so the browser and your code are in a race, and the loser is a flaky test.

## Recommended approach

Use an _explicit wait_: a loop that polls the application for a specific condition and
continues as soon as that condition is true, or raises a timeout error if it never is. You
decide what to wait for at each point where synchronisation matters, so the wait is exactly as
long as it needs to be and no longer.

Most bindings ship a library of ready-made _expected conditions_ (element visible, title
contains, alert present, and so on) that you can pass to the wait instead of writing your own
lambda. Each of them is a function that is called repeatedly until it returns a truthy value.

A fixed sleep is the first thing many people reach for, and it is nearly always wrong. It is
either too short, and the test fails on a slow machine, or too long, and every test in the
suite pays the full price every time. Likewise, do not combine an implicit wait with explicit
waits: the two timeouts add up in ways that are hard to predict.

This example waits for an element that is revealed a couple of seconds after a click:

**Java**
Example (lines L68-L69): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/waits/WaitsTest.java

**Python**
Example (lines L42-L43): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/python/tests/waits/test_waits.py

**CSharp**
Example (lines L56-L57): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/dotnet/SeleniumDocs/Waits/WaitsTest.cs

**Ruby**
Example (lines L42-L43): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/ruby/spec/waits/waits_spec.rb

**JavaScript**

**Kotlin**

## Common errors

* [NoSuchElementException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#nosuchelementexception):
  the element was looked up before it existed. Wait for it to be present or visible first.
* [StaleElementReferenceException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#staleelementreferenceexception):
  the element was found, then the page re-rendered it. Locate it again, inside the wait if necessary.
* [TimeoutException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#timeoutexception):
  the condition never became true. Check the condition and the locator before raising the timeout.
* [ElementClickInterceptedException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#elementclickinterceptedexception):
  something (often an overlay or spinner) is still covering the element. Wait for it to disappear.

## Reference

* [Waiting strategies](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/waits/): implicit and explicit waits, and how to customise them
* [Expected conditions](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/support_features/expected_conditions/)
* [Page load strategy](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/drivers/options/#pageloadstrategy): what navigation already waits for
* [Timeouts](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/drivers/options/#timeouts): the session-level timeout capabilities

# Finding elements reliably

Area: Guides
URL: https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/finding_elements/

Choosing a locator strategy that survives the next release of the application, and avoiding the ones that do not.


A locator copied out of the browser's developer tools works today and breaks the first time a
designer moves a `div`. Tests then fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the behaviour
they were written to check, and the suite stops being trusted.

## Recommended approach

Prefer locators that describe what an element _is_ over locators that describe where it
happens to sit in the document, roughly in this order:

1. **id**, when the page has stable, unique ids. This is the fastest and most readable choice.
2. **name**, for form fields, which tend to keep their names because the server depends on them.
3. **CSS selector**, for everything else. A short selector anchored on an id, a data attribute,
   or a meaningful class is both fast and expressive.
4. **Relative locators**, when the target has no stable attributes of its own but a nearby
   element does: find the input _below_ a given label, or the button _to the right of_ a field.

Avoid absolute XPath (`/html/body/div[3]/...`). It encodes the entire structure of the page, so
any change above the element breaks it, and it is slow in some browsers. XPath itself is fine
when you need it, for example to match on text content, but keep the expression short and
anchored.

If the application does not expose stable attributes, ask for them. A `data-test` attribute
costs the developers nothing and removes an entire class of failures.

Locate the first matching element:

**Java**
Example (lines L23-L24): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/elements/FindersTest.java

**Python**
Example (lines L7-L8): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/python/tests/elements/test_finders.py

**CSharp**
Example (lines L15-L16): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/dotnet/SeleniumDocs/Elements/FindersTest.cs

**Ruby**
Example (lines L10-L11): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/ruby/spec/elements/finders_spec.rb

**JavaScript**

## Common errors

* [NoSuchElementException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#nosuchelementexception):
  nothing matched. Check the locator, check that you are in the right frame, and check that the
  element exists yet (see Waiting).
* [InvalidSelectorException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#invalidselectorexception):
  the CSS or XPath expression is malformed, or an XPath expression returns something that is not an element.
* [StaleElementReferenceException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#staleelementreferenceexception):
  you held on to an element across a page update. Locate it again rather than caching it.
* [NoSuchShadowRootException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#nosuchshadowrootexception):
  the element lives inside a shadow DOM; search from the shadow root instead of the document.

## Reference

* [Locator strategies](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/elements/locators/): every strategy, including relative locators
* [Finding elements](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/elements/finders/): first match, all matches, nested searches, shadow DOM
* [Tips on working with locators](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/test_practices/encouraged/locators/)
* [Page object models](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/test_practices/encouraged/page_object_models/): keeping locators in one place

# Authentication and sessions

Area: Guides
URL: https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/authentication/

Getting past a login once, answering HTTP basic authentication prompts, and reusing a signed-in state across tests without driving the login form every time.


Almost every test starts behind a login. Driving the login form in each test is slow, it makes
every test depend on the login page working, and some forms (two-factor prompts, third-party
identity providers, CAPTCHAs) cannot be automated at all. HTTP basic authentication is a
different problem again: the browser shows a native dialog that WebDriver cannot see.

## Recommended approach

Log in through the user interface in exactly one test, the one that tests the login form.
Everywhere else, establish the session some other way and start the test already signed in.

For cookie-based sessions, navigate to the application's domain, add the session cookie with
WebDriver's cookie API, and reload. The cookie must be added while the browser is on a page in
the domain the cookie belongs to, otherwise the browser rejects it. Where the cookie comes from
is up to you: an API call that logs in, a fixture created on the server, or a value captured
from a single interactive login.

For HTTP basic authentication, use the network module of WebDriver BiDi. Register a handler
for the `authRequired` phase and answer it with the credentials; the browser never shows the
dialog. Embedding credentials in the URL (`https://user:pass@host/`) is blocked by modern
browsers and should not be relied on.

Keep tests independent: each test should set up the state it needs rather than inheriting it
from the one before, and a fresh browser per test is the simplest way to guarantee that.

Add a cookie to the current browsing context:

**Java**
Example (lines L42-L44): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/interactions/CookiesTest.java

**Python**
Example (lines L5-L9): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/python/tests/interactions/test_cookies.py

**CSharp**
Example (lines L32-L34): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/dotnet/SeleniumDocs/Interactions/CookiesTest.cs

**Ruby**
Example (lines L9-L11): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/ruby/spec/interactions/cookies_spec.rb

**JavaScript**
Example (lines L18-L21): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/javascript/test/interactions/cookies.spec.js

**Java**

**Python**
Example (lines L82): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/python/tests/bidi/test_network_commands.py

## Common errors

* [InvalidCookieDomainException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#invalidcookiedomainexception):
  the browser is not on a page in the cookie's domain. Navigate there first, then add the cookie.
* [UnableToSetCookieException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#unabletosetcookieexception):
  the cookie attributes were rejected, for example a `Secure` cookie on an `http://` page.
* [UnhandledAlertException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#unhandledalertexception):
  a basic authentication dialog is open and blocking the session. Handle it with BiDi before navigating.

## Reference

* [Working with cookies](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/interactions/cookies/)
* [BiDi network](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/w3c/network/): intercepts and the `authRequired` phase
* [Virtual authenticator](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/interactions/virtual_authenticator/): testing WebAuthn and passkeys
* [Two-factor authentication](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/test_practices/discouraged/two_factor_authentication/) and
  [third-party logins](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/test_practices/discouraged/gmail_email_and_facebook_logins/): what not to automate
* [Avoid sharing state](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/test_practices/encouraged/avoid_sharing_state/) and
  [fresh browser per test](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/test_practices/encouraged/fresh_browser_per_test/)

# Files: upload and download

Area: Guides
URL: https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/files/

Uploading a file through a form without touching the operating system's file dialog, and why downloading through the browser is not the right way to test a download.


Clicking a file input opens the operating system's file chooser, which is outside the browser
and invisible to WebDriver. Clicking a download link starts a download the API cannot watch:
there is no event for "finished", no progress, and no portable way to find the file afterwards.

## Recommended approach

**Uploads.** Do not click the input. Send the absolute path of the file to the
`<input type="file">` element with `sendKeys`, then submit the form as usual. The browser
attaches the file exactly as if it had been chosen through the dialog. The path must exist on
the machine where the _browser_ is running; when the browser is remote, on a Grid, set a local
file detector so the client uploads the file to the node first.

**Downloads.** Testing a download through the browser is discouraged. The browser's download
behaviour is configurable per browser and per platform, the file lands in a directory you then
have to poll, and none of this is what a user actually cares about. Instead, use Selenium to
get to the point where the download link exists, read its `href` (and any cookies the request
needs), and fetch it with an HTTP client in your test language. That gives you the bytes
directly, with a proper status code, and no polling.

If you are running on Selenium Grid and really need the browser to perform the download, Grid
can be configured to collect downloaded files from the node and the client can retrieve them;
see the remote WebDriver page below.

Upload a file by sending its path to the input:

**Java**
Example (lines L17-L19): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/elements/FileUploadTest.java

**Python**

## Common errors

* [InvalidArgumentException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#invalidargumentexception):
  the path does not exist on the machine running the browser. Use an absolute path, and a file
  detector when the browser is remote.
* [ElementNotInteractableException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#elementnotinteractableexception):
  the file input is hidden behind a styled button. Sending keys to a hidden file input is
  allowed in most browsers; if it is refused, check the `strictFileInteractability` capability.

# Dialogs and alerts

Area: Guides
URL: https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/dialogs/

Reading, accepting, dismissing and typing into JavaScript alerts, confirms and prompts, and deciding what should happen to a dialog your test did not expect.


A page calls `alert()`, `confirm()` or `prompt()`, the browser shows a native dialog, and
every subsequent WebDriver command fails until something closes it. If the dialog appears when
your test is not expecting it, the failure is an _unexpected alert open_ error several lines
away from the cause.

## Recommended approach

All three dialogs are handled through the same object: switch to the alert, then read its text,
accept it, dismiss it, or send keys to it. `alert()` can only be accepted; `confirm()` returns
true to the page when accepted and false when dismissed; `prompt()` additionally accepts typed
text before being accepted.

Treat the dialog like any other asynchronous event and wait for it. The bindings ship an
`alertIsPresent` expected condition that returns the alert as soon as it exists, which is both
safer and simpler than switching and catching the error.

For dialogs that may appear when no test code is ready to handle them, set the
`unhandledPromptBehavior` capability when starting the session. `dismiss` and `accept` close
the dialog silently; `dismiss and notify` (the default) and `accept and notify` close it and
raise an error so you find out; `ignore` leaves it open for you to handle. Recent drivers close
`beforeunload` prompts automatically.

With WebDriver BiDi enabled, the browsing context module also emits `userPromptOpened` and
`userPromptClosed` events, so a test can react to a dialog the moment it appears rather than
discovering it on the next command.

Switch to an alert, read its text, and close it:

**Java**
Example (lines L53-L56): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/interactions/AlertsTest.java

**Python**
Example (lines L16-L19): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/python/tests/interactions/test_alerts.py

**Ruby**
Example (lines L16-L22): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/ruby/spec/interactions/alerts_spec.rb

**JavaScript**
Example (lines L19-L21): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/javascript/test/interactions/alert.spec.js

Type into a prompt before accepting it:

**Java**
Example (lines L80-L86): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/interactions/AlertsTest.java

**Python**
Example (lines L44-L48): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/python/tests/interactions/test_alerts.py

## Common errors

* [NoAlertPresentException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#noalertpresentexception):
  you switched to an alert before it appeared, or the session's prompt handler already closed it.
  Wait for it with `alertIsPresent`, and check `unhandledPromptBehavior`.
* [UnhandledAlertException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#unhandledalertexception):
  a dialog opened that nothing handled, and the driver closed it before running your command.
  Either handle the dialog in the test or change the prompt handler.

## Reference

* [JavaScript alerts, prompts and confirmations](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/interactions/alerts/)
* [unhandledPromptBehavior](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/drivers/options/#unhandledpromptbehavior)
* [Expected conditions](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/support_features/expected_conditions/)
* [BiDi browsing context events](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/w3c/browsing_context/#user-prompt-opened-event)

# Frames and windows

Area: Guides
URL: https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/frames_and_windows/

Reaching elements inside an iframe, following a link that opens a new tab or window, and getting back to where you started.


The element is plainly visible on the page, the locator is correct, and `findElement` still
reports that it does not exist. The element is inside an `<iframe>`, or on a tab the link just
opened, and WebDriver is still looking at the document it started in.

## Recommended approach

WebDriver always has exactly one _current browsing context_: one window or tab, and within it
one frame. Commands only see that context. Switching is explicit, and you are responsible for
switching back.

**Frames.** Locate the `<iframe>` element like any other element and switch to it. You can also
switch by the frame's `name` or `id`, or by index, but a located element is the least
ambiguous. When you are done, switch to the default content to return to the top-level
document. A frame reference goes stale when the page reloads, so switch again after navigation.

**Windows and tabs.** Each window or tab has a _handle_, an opaque string. Record the current
handle before clicking a link that opens a new one, wait until the number of handles grows,
switch to the handle you have not seen before, and switch back to the original handle when
you are finished. WebDriver makes no distinction between a tab and a window. If you just need
a clean tab, open one yourself with `newWindow`; it is created already switched to.

Closing the current window leaves the session pointing at nothing, so switch to another
handle immediately after `close`. Call `quit`, not `close`, at the end of the test; it closes
every window and ends the session.

Switch into a frame using a located element:

**Java**
Example (lines L39-L41): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/interactions/FramesTest.java

**Python**

**CSharp**

## Common errors

* [NoSuchElementException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#nosuchelementexception):
  the element exists but in a different frame or window from the current one.
* [NoSuchFrameException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#nosuchframeexception):
  the frame name, id or index did not match, or the frame was removed by a navigation.
* [NoSuchWindowException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#nosuchwindowexception):
  the window you were in was closed. Switch to a handle that still exists.
* [StaleElementReferenceException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#staleelementreferenceexception):
  an element from the old frame or page is being used after a switch or reload.

## Reference

* [Working with iframes and frames](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/interactions/frames/)
* [Working with windows and tabs](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/interactions/windows/)
* [BiDi browsing context](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/w3c/browsing_context/): creating, inspecting and closing contexts with events

# Screenshots and PDFs

Area: Guides
URL: https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/screenshots/

Capturing the viewport, a single element or the whole page as an image, and printing a page to PDF.


A test fails on the CI server and the stack trace says an element was not found. What was on
the screen at the time? Without a picture, the first debugging step is to re-run the test
locally and hope it fails the same way. A screenshot taken at the moment of failure turns
that guess into evidence, and the same API is the basis of visual comparison and archiving.

## Recommended approach

WebDriver's screenshot command returns the current viewport as a PNG, Base64-encoded. Every
binding wraps that so you can save it straight to a file. Calling the same command on an
element rather than the driver crops the image to that element's bounding box, which is the
right choice when you want to compare a component rather than a whole page.

A viewport screenshot captures only what is visible without scrolling. Firefox supports a
full-page screenshot through its own driver API; with WebDriver BiDi enabled, the browsing
context module's `captureScreenshot` command works across browsers and can also capture a box
or an element.

To produce a PDF rather than an image, use the print command. It takes a `PrintOptions`
object for orientation, page ranges, size, margins, scale and whether to print background
graphics, and returns the document Base64-encoded, ready to decode and write to a file.

Attach a screenshot to every failure in your test framework's teardown hook: it is cheap,
and the one time you need it you will be glad it is there.

Take a screenshot of the viewport:

## Common errors

* [ScreenshotException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#screenshotexception):
  the browser could not capture the screen, usually because the window is minimised or the
  element is not rendered. Maximise the window or scroll the element into view.
* [StaleElementReferenceException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#staleelementreferenceexception):
  the element being captured was re-rendered between locating it and taking the screenshot.

## Reference

  [element screenshots](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/interactions/windows/#takeelementscreenshot)

# Network interception and mocking

Area: Guides
URL: https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/network/

Watching the requests a page makes, blocking or failing some of them, and answering authentication challenges, using the W3C WebDriver BiDi network module.


You want to assert that the page called an API, fail a request to see how the application
copes, block the analytics beacon that slows every test down, or supply credentials to a
basic authentication challenge. Plain WebDriver only sees the DOM; it has no view of the
traffic behind it.

## Recommended approach

Use the network module of WebDriver BiDi. It is part of the W3C standard, it works in every
browser that implements BiDi, and it is the Selenium project's supported route for anything
that needs to observe or change network traffic.

The module has two halves. _Events_ (`beforeRequestSent`, `responseStarted`,
`responseCompleted`, `authRequired`) let you subscribe to traffic and record or assert on it.
_Intercepts_ pause requests at a chosen phase so your handler can continue them, fail them,
or, at the `authRequired` phase, continue them with a username and password. Enable BiDi in
the browser options when starting the session; the reference page shows the capability for
each binding.

Keep interception narrow. Match the URL patterns you care about, remove the intercept when
the test is done, and prefer failing or stubbing an external dependency over letting the test
talk to a live third-party service.

The Chrome DevTools Protocol integration that Selenium offered before BiDi existed is
Chromium-only, tied to specific browser versions, and being phased out. Do not start new work
on it.

Subscribe to requests as they are sent:

**Java**
Example (lines L30-L35): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/bidirectional/webdriver_bidi/NetworkEventsTest.java

**Python**
Example (lines L68-L71): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/python/tests/bidi/test_network_commands.py

**JavaScript**
Example (lines L24-L27): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/javascript/test/bidirectional/network_events.spec.js

Intercept a request and fail it:

**Java**
Example (lines L99-L101): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/bidirectional/webdriver_bidi/NetworkCommandsTest.java

**Python**
Example (lines L46-L49): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/python/tests/bidi/test_network_commands.py

**Java**
Example (lines L55-L60): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/bidirectional/webdriver_bidi/NetworkCommandsTest.java

**Python**
Example (lines L82): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/python/tests/bidi/test_network_commands.py

**JavaScript**
Example (lines L43-L45): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/javascript/test/bidirectional/network_commands.spec.js

## Common errors

* [TimeoutException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#timeoutexception):
  an intercepted request was never continued or failed, so navigation hung until the page load
  timeout. Every intercepted request needs a handler that resolves it.
* [UnsupportedCommandException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#unsupportedcommandexception):
  BiDi was not enabled for the session, or the browser does not implement the command yet.

## Reference

* [BiDi network](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/w3c/network/): all commands and events
* [Enabling BiDi](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/_index/#enabling-bidi-in-selenium)
* [Mock external services](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/test_practices/encouraged/mock_external_services/)
* [HTTP response codes](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/test_practices/discouraged/http_response_codes/): why WebDriver does not expose them directly

# Console and logs

Area: Guides
URL: https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/logging/

Capturing the browser's console output and JavaScript errors with BiDi, and turning up Selenium's own logging to see what the bindings and the driver are doing.


Something went wrong, and the only evidence is a failed assertion. There are three separate
streams of information that could explain it: what the page wrote to the browser console,
what exception JavaScript threw, and what Selenium itself was sending to and receiving from
the driver. By default you see none of them.

## Recommended approach

**Browser console and JavaScript errors.** With WebDriver BiDi enabled, the log module streams
console entries and uncaught JavaScript exceptions to your test as they happen. Register a
handler before the action you want to observe, then assert on the entries it collects. This
is the cross-browser, standards-based replacement for the old Chromium-only log retrieval,
and it catches errors the page swallowed before a user would have seen them.

**Selenium's own logging.** Each binding logs through its language's standard logging
facility: `java.util.logging` in Java, the `logging` module in Python, Selenium's `Log` class
in .NET, and `Selenium::WebDriver.logger` in Ruby. Raising the level to debug shows every
command sent to the driver and every response, which is usually enough to tell whether the
problem is in your code, the driver or the browser. Logs go to the console by default; add a
file handler to keep them with the rest of your test artifacts.

**Driver logs.** The browser driver (chromedriver, geckodriver, and so on) keeps its own log,
configured through the driver's service class. Reach for it when the browser fails to start or
crashes mid-session.

Collect console messages with BiDi:

**Java**
Example (lines L30-L39): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/bidirectional/webdriver_bidi/LogTest.java

**Python**
Example (lines L11-L15): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/python/tests/bidi/test_bidi_logging.py

**JavaScript**
Example (lines L23-L31): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/javascript/test/bidirectional/logInspector.spec.js

**Java**

## Common errors

* [JavascriptException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#javascriptexception):
  a script you executed through WebDriver threw. The BiDi log module shows the page's own
  errors, which this exception does not cover.
* [UnsupportedCommandException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#unsupportedcommandexception):
  BiDi was not enabled for the session, so the log module is unavailable.

## Reference

* [BiDi log](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/w3c/log/): console entries and JavaScript exceptions
* [Logging Selenium commands](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/logging/): levels, output and filtering per binding
* [Driver service](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/drivers/service/): where the driver's own log goes
* [Enabling BiDi](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/bidi/_index/#enabling-bidi-in-selenium)

# Running in CI

Area: Guides
URL: https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/ci/

Running a Selenium suite on a build server: headless browsers, driver management without manual downloads, and when to move to Grid or Docker.


The suite passes on your laptop and fails on the build server. The server has no display, a
different browser version, no driver on the `PATH`, and a locked-down network. Each of those
is a separate failure with a separate fix, and the error messages rarely say which one you
have hit.

## Recommended approach

**No display.** Run the browser headless. Chrome and Edge take the `--headless=new` argument,
Firefox takes `-headless`. The page renders the same way, so only the browser options change.
Keep headless behind a configuration flag so you can still watch a test locally.

**No driver.** Do not download driver binaries in your pipeline. Selenium Manager, which
ships with Selenium 4.6 and later, detects the installed browser, downloads the matching
driver, and caches it in `~/.cache/selenium`; cache that directory between runs. Some hosted
runners pre-install drivers on the `PATH`, and a stale one there takes precedence over
Selenium Manager, so remove it or keep it current.

**Locked-down network.** Selenium Manager needs to reach the browser vendors' download
endpoints the first time. Behind a proxy, set it with the `SE_PROXY` environment variable or
the Selenium Manager configuration file.

**Scale.** When one runner starting one browser per test becomes too slow, point the same
tests at a Selenium Grid and run them in parallel without
changing the test code.

Collect a screenshot and the Selenium log on every failure; a CI failure without artifacts
is a re-run waiting to happen.

Start a headless browser:

**Java**

A minimal GitHub Actions workflow, shown for Python, is a starting point only. The hosted
Ubuntu runner already has Chrome and Firefox installed; the only Selenium-specific step is
installing the binding:

```yaml
name: tests
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: pip install selenium pytest
      - run: pytest
```

The same shape applies to every binding: check out, install the language toolchain, install
the Selenium package, run the standard test command.

## Common errors

* [Unable to locate driver](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/driver_location/):
  Selenium Manager could not find or download a driver. Check the browser is installed and the
  network allows the download.
* [SessionNotCreatedException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#sessionnotcreatedexception):
  the driver on the `PATH` does not match the installed browser, or the browser cannot start
  without a display. Remove stale drivers and run headless.
* [InvalidArgumentException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#invalidargumentexception):
  a browser option is wrong for this browser or version, for example a user data directory that is already in use by another session.

## Reference

* [Browser options](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/drivers/options/) and the per-browser pages for
  [Chrome](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/browsers/chrome/),
  [Edge](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/browsers/edge/) and
  [Firefox](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/browsers/firefox/)
* [Selenium Manager](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/selenium_manager/): caching, proxies and offline use
* [Grid getting started](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/grid/getting_started/)
* [Test practices](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/test_practices/_index/): keeping tests independent so they can run in parallel

# Running in Docker and Grid

Area: Guides
URL: https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/docker_and_grid/

Moving the browser off the machine that runs the tests, with Selenium Grid and the project's Docker images, so a suite can run in parallel and against several browsers.


A suite that takes an hour because every test starts its own browser on the same machine.
A requirement to test on a browser that is not installed where the tests run. A build server
that must not have a browser on it at all. In each case the browser needs to be somewhere
other than the test process.

## Recommended approach

Selenium Grid is a server that accepts WebDriver sessions over HTTP and routes them to
browsers it manages. Your test code changes in exactly one place: instead of constructing a
local driver, construct a remote one with the Grid URL and the browser options. Everything
else stays the same, so a suite can run locally during development and on a Grid in CI with a
single configuration switch.

**Standalone** mode runs the whole Grid in one process and is the right starting point. It
needs a Java runtime and the Selenium Server jar, listens on `http://localhost:4444`, and can
use Selenium Manager to fetch drivers for the browsers it finds. **Hub and Node** spreads
browsers across several machines, and **distributed** mode separates each Grid component for
large installations.

The quickest way to get a Grid, and the only way to get one with no browser on the host, is
the project's own Docker images in the
[docker-selenium](https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/docker-selenium) repository. They package the
Grid, a browser and its driver, and are published for each Selenium release. A single
`docker run` gives you a standalone Grid with Chrome, Firefox or Edge; the repository also has
Docker Compose and Kubernetes examples, video recording, and VNC for watching a session.

When the browser is remote, files to upload must reach the node first, through a file
detector, and downloads must be enabled on the Grid and fetched back through the client. Both
are covered on the remote WebDriver page.

Point a test at a Grid:

**Java**
Example (lines L38-L39): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/java/src/test/java/dev/selenium/drivers/RemoteWebDriverTest.java

**Python**
Example (lines L13-L14): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/python/tests/drivers/test_remote_webdriver.py

**CSharp**
Example (lines L28-L29): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/dotnet/SeleniumDocs/Drivers/RemoteWebDriverTest.cs

**Ruby**
Example (lines L20-L21): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/ruby/spec/drivers/remote_webdriver_spec.rb

**JavaScript**
Example (lines L43-L44): https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/seleniumhq.github.io/blob/trunk/examples/javascript/test/drivers/remote_webdriver.spec.js

## Common errors

* [SessionNotCreatedException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#sessionnotcreatedexception):
  no node on the Grid can satisfy the requested browser and version. Check the Grid's status
  page at the Grid URL for the capabilities it offers.
* [InvalidArgumentException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#invalidargumentexception):
  a local file path was sent to a remote browser. Set a file detector so the file is uploaded.
* [WebDriverException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#webdriverexception)
  with a connection error: the Grid URL is wrong, the server is not running, or a firewall is
  between the client and the Grid.

## Reference

* [Grid getting started](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/grid/getting_started/): standalone, hub and node, distributed
* [Grid configuration](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/grid/configuration/_index/) and
  [advanced features](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/grid/advanced_features/_index/)
* [Remote WebDriver](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/drivers/remote_webdriver/): file uploads and downloads with a Grid
* [docker-selenium](https://github.com/SeleniumHQ/docker-selenium): the project's Docker images and deployment examples

# Debugging a failing test

Area: Guides
URL: https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/guides/debugging/

A short procedure for working out why a Selenium test failed: read the exception, gather evidence, and narrow the cause before changing anything.


A test that used to pass now fails, or passes locally and fails in CI, or fails one run in
five. The temptation is to add a sleep, re-run, and move on. That hides the cause, and the
test comes back.

## Recommended approach

**Read the exception first.** The W3C WebDriver specification defines a fixed set of errors,
and each one points at a specific cause. _No such element_ means the locator matched nothing
in the current frame at that moment. _Stale element reference_ means the page replaced the
element after you found it. _Element click intercepted_ means something was drawn on top of
it. _Session not created_ means the browser never started. The common errors page lists every
one with its likely cause and fixes; start there before reading any code.

**Gather evidence at the moment of failure.** Add a hook to your test framework that, on
failure, saves a screenshot alongside the Selenium log. The screenshot shows what the page
looked like; the log shows what Selenium sent and what the driver replied. With BiDi enabled
you can also collect the browser console and any JavaScript exceptions, which often explain a
page that looks right but does not respond.

**Narrow the cause.** Ask, in order:

1. Is it timing? Most intermittent failures are. Replace any sleep with an explicit wait for
   the condition the next line depends on, and check that an implicit wait is not also set.
2. Is it the locator? Try it in the browser's developer tools, and check whether the element
   is inside a frame or a shadow root.
3. Is it the environment? A different browser version, a stale driver on the `PATH`, no
   display on the build server, or a blocked download endpoint all produce failures that never
   happen locally.
4. Is it the application? Then the test has found a bug, which is what it was for.

**Reproduce before you fix.** Run the test on its own, then in the full suite. A test that
only fails in the suite is sharing state with another test, usually through a reused browser
or a cookie left behind.

## Common errors

The [common errors](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/) page
covers each error in detail. The ones you will meet most often:

* [NoSuchElementException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#nosuchelementexception)
* [StaleElementReferenceException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#staleelementreferenceexception)
* [ElementClickInterceptedException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#elementclickinterceptedexception)
* [TimeoutException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#timeoutexception)
* [SessionNotCreatedException](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/_index/#sessionnotcreatedexception)
* [Unable to locate driver](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/webdriver/troubleshooting/errors/driver_location/)

## Reference

* Waiting, Finding elements and
  Frames and windows: the three guides behind most failures
* Screenshots: capturing the page on failure
* Console and logs: Selenium's log and the browser console
* Running in CI: failures that only happen on the build server
* [Test practices](https://www.selenium.dev/documentation/test_practices/_index/): the discouraged patterns that cause flaky tests
